app.subtitle: How does Earth's orbit shift the apparent positions of nearby stars?

help.title: Welcome to the Stellar Parallax Simulator
help.intro: Explore annual parallax — the small yearly shift of nearby stars caused by Earth's orbit — from three viewpoints and with live graphs.
stepTitles: When Earth moves, the sky shifts
Set up stars and check the graphs
stepBodies: Earth circles the Sun once a year. Because we look from a different place, a nearby star appears to shift slightly against the distant background stars. This is annual parallax.
Use the tabs at the top of the view to switch between Overhead, From Earth and From Star. The bar below the view plays, pauses and steps through the months.
In the Stars tab on the left you can change distance and direction (ecliptic latitude/longitude) or add real stars. You can also click the graphs to change the date or the distance.
The learning panel on the right has explanations, guided missions, a measurement challenge and a quiz. Work through the missions from top to bottom to build understanding step by step.

shape.circle: Ecliptic latitude β = {{beta}}°: close to the ecliptic pole, so the apparent motion is almost a circle.
shape.line: Ecliptic latitude β = {{beta}}°: close to the ecliptic plane, so the star moves back and forth along a line.
shape.ellipse: Ecliptic latitude β = {{beta}}°: the star traces an ellipse (minor / major axis = |sin β| = {{ratio}}).

explain.now: Around {{month}}. The star appears shifted from its direction as seen from the Sun by {{pct}}% of the maximum shift p.

view.overhead: Overhead: extend the line of sight (yellow) from Earth (blue) through the star; where it hits the background sky traces an ellipse over a year. That is the apparent motion.
view.observer: From Earth: + marks the direction seen from the Sun. Distant background stars stay put; only nearby stars trace ellipses.
view.stellar: From Star: seen from the star, Earth circles the Sun in a tiny ellipse. Its largest angular separation is p.

explain.tipNear: A very nearby star: large parallax and a large wobble.
explain.tipFar: A distant star: the parallax is tiny and the star barely moves. Precision space telescopes are needed.
explain.tipCompare: The largest shift (2p = {{v}}) is between {{m1}} and {{m2}}.
explain.tipTryCompare: Turn on the half-year comparison (key C) to measure how far the star shifts in six months.
explain.tipAddStar: Add another star to compare the wobble of near and far stars at the same scale.

what.title: What is annual parallax?
what.body: Earth orbits the Sun at a radius of 1 AU (about 150 million km). Because our viewpoint moves, nearby stars appear to shift slightly against distant stars. The largest angle subtended by the Sun–Earth distance (1 AU) as seen from the star is called the annual parallax p.

parsec.title: The parsec (pc)
parsec.body: One parsec is the distance at which the annual parallax is exactly 1″ (1/3600 of a degree). The name comes from parallax + second. Distance d [pc] and parallax p [″] are simply related by d = 1/p.
parsec.scale: Sense of scale: if the Sun–Earth distance were 1 cm, 1 pc would be about 2 km away — and even the nearest star would be about 2.7 km away.

shape.title: The shape of the apparent motion
shape.body: The apparent motion has the shape of Earth's orbit as seen from the star. Stars at an ecliptic pole (β = ±90°) trace circles, stars on the ecliptic (β = 0°) move back and forth along a line, and others trace ellipses. The semi-major axis is always p.
shape.twoP: The largest shift between two dates six months apart is 2p. Remember to halve it when reading p from a graph!

aberration.title: Parallax vs. annual aberration
aberration.body: Earth moves at about 30 km/s. Just as rain seems to come from ahead when you run, starlight appears tilted toward the direction of motion (annual aberration). In 1729 Bradley discovered it while searching for parallax.

phase.label: Timing
phase.parallax: Max when Earth is at right angles to the star

precision.title: Precision and measurable distance
precision.body: The smaller the parallax an instrument can measure, the farther it can measure distances (max distance ≈ 1 / precision).
precision.naked: With the naked eye (resolution about 1′ = 60″) no stellar parallax is visible — telescopes were needed to discover it.

history.title: A short history
history.items:
Antiquity|The absence of visible parallax was used as an argument that Earth does not move
1543|Copernicus proposes heliocentrism and argues the stars are so far away that their parallax is tiny
1729|Searching for parallax, Bradley discovers annual aberration
1838|Bessel makes the first parallax measurement: 61 Cygni, about 0.31″
1989|The Hipparcos satellite measures parallaxes of about 120,000 stars to about 0.001″
2013|The Gaia satellite launches and measures parallaxes of over a billion stars

model.title: Simplifications in this model
model.body: Earth's orbit is a circle; proper motion, binary motion and atmospheric refraction are ignored. Distances and angles in the 3D view are exaggerated for visibility. Dates assume Earth's heliocentric ecliptic longitude is about 100° on January 1.

missions.title: Observation missions
missions.intro: Work from top to bottom. Missions are checked off automatically as you explore.
missions.allDone: 🎉 All missions complete! You are a parallax master.

playYear.title: Let Earth complete one orbit (one year)
playYear.hint: Press ▶ Play below the view and watch for a full year.
playYear.learned: The apparent position returns to where it started every year.

observer.title: Watch the star from Earth
observer.hint: Choose the From Earth tab above the view (key 2). Compare the background stars with the nearby star.
observer.learned: Distant background stars stay put; only nearby stars shift.

compare.title: Find the largest shift with the half-year comparison
compare.hint: Turn on Half-year comparison in the Display tab (key C). Move the date to find when the shift is largest.
compare.learned: The largest shift between dates six months apart is 2p; the parallax p is half of it.

distance.title: Change the distance and watch the parallax
distance.hint: Use the distance slider or the Distance ×2 button in the Stars tab.
distance.learned: Doubling the distance halves the parallax: p = 1/d.

multi.title: Add stars to compare near and far
multi.hint: Use “Add a real star” in the Stars tab — try Proxima Centauri and Deneb.
multi.learned: At the same scale, nearer stars clearly wobble more.

pole.title: Set ecliptic latitude to 90° (the pole)
pole.hint: Choose “Pole 90°” under ecliptic latitude. Watch the shape of the path!
pole.learned: A star at the ecliptic pole traces a circle.

ecliptic.title: Set ecliptic latitude to 0° (on the ecliptic)
ecliptic.hint: Press “Ecliptic 0°”. What shape is the path now?
ecliptic.learned: A star on the ecliptic moves back and forth along a line.

graphClick.title: Click the graphs
graphClick.hint: Click the “Over time” graph to change the date, or the “Parallax vs distance” graph to change the distance.
graphClick.learned: The shift is a yearly wave, and p is inversely proportional to distance.

stellar.title: Look back at the solar system from the star
stellar.hint: Choose the From Star tab above the view (key 3).
stellar.learned: The largest Sun–Earth angle seen from a star is that star's parallax p.

aberration.title: Compare with annual aberration
aberration.hint: Turn on Annual aberration in the Display tab (key A) and look at From Earth and the Over time graph.
aberration.learned: Aberration is about 20.5″ regardless of distance, and is three months out of step with parallax.

challenge.title: Solve a measurement challenge
challenge.hint: In the Measure tab, find the distance of a mystery star from its path.
challenge.learned: Read p from the graph and d = 1/p gives the distance.

quiz.title: Get 4 or more right in the quiz
quiz.hint: Try the Quiz tab in the learning panel.
quiz.learned: You've mastered the basics of stellar parallax!

challenge.intro: This is a mystery star's apparent motion over one year (grid in arcseconds ″). Read the parallax p from the path and work out the distance d.
challenge.plotLabel: Apparent path of the mystery star
challenge.hintText: The parallax p is the distance from the center (where the axes cross) to the farthest point of the path — two points six months apart are 2p apart. Enter p and tap outside the box to fill in d = 1/p automatically.

quiz.tryAgain: Read the explanations and try again.

distFromParallax.question: A star has an annual parallax of {{p}}″. How far away is it in parsecs?

parallaxFromDist.question: A star is {{d}} pc away. What is its annual parallax in arcseconds?

whichCloser.question: Star A has a parallax of {{pa}}″ and star B {{pb}}″. Which is closer to Earth?
whichCloser.explanation: The larger the parallax, the closer the star. {{star}} is closer, at {{d}} pc.

halfYearShift.question: A star's apparent position differs by at most {{sep}}″ between two dates six months apart. How far away is it?
halfYearShift.explanation: Six months apart Earth has moved across its orbit (2 AU), so the shift is 2p. p = {{sep}} ÷ 2 = {{p}}″ and d = 1/p = {{d}} pc.

precisionLimit.question: An instrument can measure parallaxes down to {{lim}}″. Up to roughly what distance can it measure?
precisionLimit.explanation: The smallest measurable parallax is {{lim}}″, so d = 1 / {{lim}} = {{d}} pc.

parsecDef.question: Which is the correct definition of one parsec?
choices: The distance at which the annual parallax is 1 arcsecond
The distance light travels in one year
The distance at which the annual parallax is 1 degree
parsecDef.explanation: 1 pc is the distance at which the parallax is 1″ — about 3.26 light-years (about 206,265 AU).

doubleDistance.question: If the distance to a star doubles, what happens to its annual parallax?
doubleDistance.explanation: Since p = 1/d, parallax is inversely proportional to distance. Twice as far means half the parallax.

lightYear.question: About how many light-years is one parsec?
lightYear.explanation: 1 pc ≈ 3.26 light-years ≈ 206,265 AU (206,265 is one radian expressed in arcseconds).

poleShape.question: What shape does a star at the ecliptic pole (latitude 90°) trace over a year due to parallax?
poleShape.explanation: Seen from the ecliptic pole, Earth's orbit looks circular, so the apparent motion is a circle. Lower latitudes give flatter ellipses.

eclipticShape.question: What is the parallax motion of a star on the ecliptic (latitude 0°)?
choices: Back and forth along a line
eclipticShape.explanation: Seen edge-on, Earth's orbit looks like a line segment, so the apparent motion is back and forth along a line.

background.question: Seen from Earth, why do the background stars hardly move?
choices: They are so far away that their parallax is tiny
They are inside the solar system
They don't shine on their own
background.explanation: Parallax is inversely proportional to distance. Very distant stars have unmeasurably small parallaxes, so they serve as fixed reference points.

aberration.question: Which statement about annual aberration is correct?
choices: Every star shifts by up to about 20.5″, regardless of distance
aberration.explanation: Aberration depends on the ratio of Earth's orbital speed to the speed of light (about 1/10,000), not on the star's distance.

evidence.question: Observing annual parallax is mainly evidence for what?
evidence.explanation: Parallax arises because Earth's orbital motion changes our viewpoint. Bessel's 1838 measurement was direct evidence of Earth's orbit (as was annual aberration).

naked.question: The naked eye can resolve about 1′ (60″). Which stars show annual parallax to the naked eye?
choices: None — the largest is only about 0.77″
naked.explanation: Even Proxima Centauri's parallax is only about 0.77″, roughly 1/80 of the eye's resolution. That is why parallax was not found until telescopes improved.

presetNote.proxima: The nearest star to the Sun (a red dwarf) — the largest known stellar parallax.
presetNote.alphaCen: The main star of Proxima's triple system; the nearest star visible to the naked eye.
presetNote.barnard: The star with the largest proper motion (about 10″ per year). Note: proper motion is not modeled here.
presetNote.sirius: The brightest star in the night sky (Canis Major).
presetNote.cyg61: In 1838 Bessel made the first-ever parallax measurement on this star.
presetNote.altair: One of the Summer Triangle stars, in Aquila.
presetNote.vega: One of the Summer Triangle stars, in Lyra. Its high ecliptic latitude gives a rounded ellipse.
presetNote.aldebaran: The bright star of Taurus. Lying near the ecliptic (β ≈ −5°), it moves almost along a line.
presetNote.polaris: The North Star. Its parallax (about 0.0075″) is too small for ground telescopes to measure well.
presetNote.betelgeuse: Orion's red supergiant. Its parallax is about 0.006″ and its exact distance is still debated.
presetNote.deneb: One of the Summer Triangle stars. Very distant (about 800 pc), with a parallax of only about 1 mas.
